proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be the given similar plane numbers, and let P be their product. Choose the direct mean-proportional route, since VIII.18 applies immediately to the hypothesis: there is a number M such that A:M = M:B. [8.18]

**Step 2.** Apply VII.19 to the four proportional numbers A, M, M, B. The product of the first and fourth equals the product of the second and third. Hence P = A·B = M·M. [7.19]

**Step 3.** A number produced by multiplying a number by itself is a square number. Since P = M·M, the product of the two given similar plane numbers is square. [D7.18]
statement: If two similar plane numbers by multiplying one another make some number, the product will be square.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be numbers whose product is square. By the definition of a square number, there is a number C such that AB = CC. [D7.18]

**Step 2.** Take the direct route through a mean proportional. Apply the converse of VII.19 to the four numbers A, C, C, B: since the product of the first and fourth equals that of the second and third, A:C = C:B. Thus C is a mean proportional between A and B. [7.19]

**Step 3.** Numbers between which there is one mean proportional are similar plane numbers. Therefore A and B are similar plane numbers, as required. [8.20]
statement: If two numbers by multiplying one another make a square number, they are similar plane numbers.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the given cube. By the definition of a cube, there is a number a such that, on putting b = a·a, we have A = a·b. [D7.19] We use the four-term cube criterion, since it allows the given cube A to be the first term of a continued proportion. [8.23]

**Step 2.** Multiplication of a and b by a produces b and A respectively. Therefore
 a:b = b:A. [7.17]

**Step 3.** Put D = b·b, E = b·A, and F = A·A. Commutativity gives b·a = A and A·b = E. [7.16] Multiplying a and b by b, multiplying b and A by b, and multiplying b and A by A, respectively, gives
 A:D = a:b,
 D:E = b:A,
 E:F = b:A. [7.17]
Together with Step 2, these equalities show that A:D = D:E = E:F. Thus A, D, E, F are four numbers in continued proportion.

**Step 4.** Since the first number A is a cube, the fourth number F is also a cube. [8.23] But F = A·A. Therefore a cube number multiplied by itself produces a cube, as required.
statement: If a cube number by multiplying itself make some number, the product will be cube.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be cube numbers, and let C be the product made by A multiplying B. Let D be the product made by A multiplying itself. Since A is cube, D is cube. [9.3]

**Step 2.** Multiplication of A and B by the same number A gives D and C respectively. Therefore D:C = A:B. [7.17]

**Step 3.** Apply the cube-ratio criterion directly, since Step 2 supplies precisely its ratio hypothesis: D and C have to one another the ratio of the cube numbers A and B, and D is cube. Hence C is cube. Thus a cube number multiplying a cube number produces a cube number. [8.25]
statement: If a cube number by multiplying a cube number make some number, the product will be cube.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the cube number A, by multiplying the number B, produce the cube number C. Let a and c be the respective sides of these cubes. Thus A = a³, C = c³, and AB = C. [D7.19]

**Step 2.** Since AB = C, A measures C. We use the direct side-divisibility theorem, since the hypothesis already supplies this measurement: because the cube A measures the cube C, its side a measures the side c. Let d be the number of times that a measures c; then c = ad. [D7.15, 8.15]

**Step 3.** Regrouping the repeated sums defining multiplication and interchanging factors gives
C = c³ = (ad)(ad)(ad) = (aaa)(ddd) = A·d³.
Consequently AB = A·d³, since both products equal C. [D7.15, 7.16, CN1]

**Step 4.** Hence B = d³. Indeed, if either B or d³ were greater, its A-fold sum would contain the other's A-fold sum as a proper part and would therefore be greater, contrary to their equality. Thus B is the product of three equal numbers d, and so is a cube. Therefore, if a cube number multiplying a number produces a cube, the multiplied number is also a cube. [D7.15, CN5, D7.19]
statement: If a cube number by multiplying any number make a cube number, the multiplied number will also be cube.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the given number, and let B = A·A be cube, as hypothesized. Form C = B·A. Since C = (A·A)·A is contained by three equal numbers, C is cube. [D7.19]

**Step 2.** Apply the cube-factor criterion directly, since both the factor B and the product C are cube: B, by multiplying A, makes the cube number C. Therefore the multiplied number A is itself cube, as required. [9.5]
statement: If a number by multiplying itself make a cube number, it will itself also be cube.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the composite number A, by multiplying any number B, produce C. We use the definitions directly, since it suffices to exhibit three numerical factors of C [D7.17]. Since A is composite, choose a proper numerical measure D of A, and let E be the number of times D measures A [D7.13].

**Step 2.** By the definition of multiplication, E multiplying D produces A. Therefore, multiplying E and D, and then multiplying their product A by B, produces C [D7.15 and the hypothesis].

**Step 3.** Thus the three numbers E, D, and B, by successive multiplication, produce C. By the definition of a solid number, C is solid, as required [D7.17].
statement: If a composite number by multiplying any number make some number, the product will be solid.

proof:
**Step 1.** Write the given progression as u, a₁, a₂, …, aₙ, where u is the unit; thus aⱼ occupies position j+1. All assertions below concern terms that exist. We choose the direct route of comparing equally spaced blocks and then applying the definitions of square and cube, since these comparisons supply the required equal factors. [D7.1; 7.14; D7.18; D7.19]

**Step 2.** Put a=a₁. Continued proportion gives u:a = aⱼ:aⱼ₊₁. Hence aⱼ measures aⱼ₊₁ as many times as the unit measures a. By VII.15, alternately, a measures aⱼ₊₁ as many times as the unit measures aⱼ. Consequently,
a:aⱼ₊₁ = u:aⱼ.
This holds for every j≥1 for which aⱼ₊₁ exists. [D7.20; 7.15]

**Step 3.** Let m≥1 and suppose a₂ₘ exists. Compare the two blocks of numbers
a₁, a₂, …, aₘ₊₁ and aₘ, aₘ₊₁, …, a₂ₘ.
Their corresponding successive ratios are equal. Therefore, ex aequali,
aₘ:a₂ₘ = a₁:aₘ₊₁ = u:aₘ,
where the last equality is Step 2. If a₃ₘ also exists, comparing the first block with a₂ₘ, a₂ₘ₊₁, …, a₃ₘ similarly gives
a₂ₘ:a₃ₘ = a₁:aₘ₊₁ = u:aₘ.
These applications involve blocks consisting entirely of numbers, not the unit. [7.14]

**Step 4.** From u:aₘ = aₘ:a₂ₘ, the number aₘ measures a₂ₘ as many times as the unit measures aₘ. Thus a₂ₘ is produced by multiplying aₘ by itself, and is square. Likewise, from u:aₘ = a₂ₘ:a₃ₘ, the number a₃ₘ is produced by multiplying that square by aₘ, and is therefore cube. As m ranges over the positive integers, the square terms occupy positions 3, 5, 7, …, successively leaving out one; the cube terms occupy positions 4, 7, 10, …, successively leaving out two. [D7.20; D7.15; D7.18; D7.19]

**Step 5.** For every positive integer k with a₆ₖ present, Step 4 with m=3k shows that a₆ₖ is square, while Step 4 with m=2k shows that the same term is cube. These terms occupy positions 7, 13, 19, …, successively leaving out five. Hence the seventh term is both square and cube, as is every term obtained thereafter by leaving out five. Together with Step 4, this proves every assertion. [D7.18; D7.19]
statement: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, the third from the unit will be square, as will also those which successively leave out one; the fourth will be cube, as will also all those which leave out two; and the seventh will be at once cube and square, as will also those which leave out five.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the continued proportion be 1, A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ, with A₁ square by hypothesis. If n = 1, there is nothing further to prove. Otherwise A₂, the third term counting the unit, is square by Proposition 9.8. Thus A₁ and A₂ are both square. [9.8]

**Step 2.** Choose the direct square-ratio propagation route: A₁:A₂ is now a ratio of two square numbers. By continued proportion, every successive pair Aᵢ, Aᵢ₊₁ has this same ratio. Proposition 8.24 therefore implies that whenever Aᵢ is square, Aᵢ₊₁ is also square. [8.24]

**Step 3.** Beginning with the given square A₁ and applying Step 2 successively through the finite sequence, every Aᵢ is square. Hence, if the number after the unit is square, all the remaining numbers in the continued proportion are also square. [8.24]
statement: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be square, all the rest will also be square.

proof:
**Step 1.** Write the given progression as A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ, where A₁ is the unit and A₂ is not square. By IX.8, A₃, A₅, A₇, and all subsequent terms in alternate positions are square. It remains to exclude squares in the even positions. [9.8]

**Step 2.** Use VIII.22 on reversed consecutive triples: this is the direct route because it transfers squareness two positions backward without constructing any auxiliary numbers. For every j ≥ 4, continued proportion gives
Aⱼ₋₂ : Aⱼ₋₁ = Aⱼ₋₁ : Aⱼ.
By the definition of numerical proportionality, reversing these ratios gives
Aⱼ : Aⱼ₋₁ = Aⱼ₋₁ : Aⱼ₋₂.
Thus Aⱼ, Aⱼ₋₁, Aⱼ₋₂ are also in continued proportion. If Aⱼ is square, VIII.22 therefore makes Aⱼ₋₂ square. [D7.20, 8.22]

**Step 3.** Suppose an even-positioned term A₂ᵣ, with r ≥ 2, were square. Repeatedly applying Step 2 would make A₂ᵣ₋₂, A₂ᵣ₋₄, and eventually A₂ square, contrary to the hypothesis. Hence no even-positioned term is square; A₂ itself is already excluded by hypothesis. Together with Step 1, this proves that among the numbers after the unit, precisely the third from the unit and those successively leaving out one are square. [8.22, 9.8]
statement: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be not square, neither will any other be square except the third from the unit and all those which leave out one.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the given continued proportion be
\(1,A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n\), where \(1\) denotes the unit. Since \(A_1\) is a multitude of units and every consecutive pair has the ratio \(1:A_1\), the terms increase. Choose any two of the numbers, the less \(A_i\) and the greater \(A_j\), so that \(i<j\), and put \(d=j-i\). Then \(1\le d\le n-1\), so both \(A_d\) and \(A_{d+1}\) occur in the given progression. [D7.2, D7.3, D7.20]

**Step 2.** By continued proportion,
\[
1:A_1=A_d:A_{d+1}.
\]
The unit measures \(A_1\) according to \(A_1\); hence \(A_d\) measures \(A_{d+1}\) the same number of times. Apply VII.15, choosing this alternation rule because it explicitly concerns a unit: the unit measures \(A_d\) the same number of times that \(A_1\) measures \(A_{d+1}\). Therefore \(A_1\) measures \(A_{d+1}\) according to \(A_d\). [D7.2, D7.3, D7.20, 7.15]

**Step 3.** Consider the two blocks of numbers
\[
A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_{d+1}
\quad\text{and}\quad
A_i,A_{i+1},\ldots,A_j.
\]
They have equal length, and their corresponding consecutive ratios are equal by the given continued proportion. Thus VII.14 applies directly to these blocks and gives, ex aequali,
\[
A_1:A_{d+1}=A_i:A_j.
\]
[7.14]

**Step 4.** Since \(A_1\) measures \(A_{d+1}\) according to \(A_d\), equality of these ratios means that \(A_i\) likewise measures \(A_j\) according to \(A_d\). This is one of the numbers in the given progression. If the less term chosen is the initial unit itself, it measures any greater term according to that very term. Consequently, in every case the less measures the greater according to one of the numbers having a place among the proportional numbers, as required. [D7.20, D7.3, D7.2]
statement: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, the less measures the greater according to some one of the numbers which have place among the proportional numbers.

proof:
**Step 1.** Write the given continued proportion as \(1,A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n\), where \(A_1\) is next to the unit. We take the direct successive-product route, because the common ratio determines each term from its predecessor. For every \(k\geq2\),
\[
1:A_1=A_{k-1}:A_k.
\]
Since a number consists of units, the unit measures \(A_1\) as many times as there are units in \(A_1\). By the definition of numerical proportion, \(A_{k-1}\) measures \(A_k\) that same number of times. Thus, by the definition of multiplication,
\[
A_k=A_1A_{k-1}.
\]
[D7.2, D7.20, D7.15]

**Step 2.** Let \(p\) be any prime number measuring the last term \(A_n\). If \(n=1\), it already measures the number next to the unit. Otherwise, since \(A_n=A_1A_{n-1}\), VII.30 shows that \(p\) measures either \(A_1\) or \(A_{n-1}\). If it measures \(A_1\), the assertion follows. If not, apply the same theorem to the preceding product, and continue backwards. This finite process must reach \(A_2=A_1A_1\), where VII.30 necessarily gives that \(p\) measures \(A_1\). Hence every prime number measuring the last term also measures the number next to the unit. Therefore, by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit is measured by the same. [7.30]
statement: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit will also be measured by the same.

proof:
**Step 1.** Write the given continued proportion as
\[
a_0=1,\quad a_1=p,\quad a_2,\ldots,a_n,
\]
where \(p\) is prime and \(a_n\) is the greatest term. Since \(1:p=a_i:a_{i+1}\), each term after the unit is obtained by multiplying its predecessor by \(p\):
\[
a_{i+1}=p a_i.
\]
[D7.20, D7.15]

**Step 2.** Suppose that a number \(d\) measures \(a_n\) but is not any term of the progression. The unit measures \(d\), since a number is composed of units. Choose the last term \(a_k\) of the progression which measures \(d\), allowing \(a_0=1\). Because \(d\) measures and is unequal to \(a_n\), we have \(d<a_n\); hence \(k<n\). Write
\[
d=a_k q.
\]
Since \(d\ne a_k\), the quotient \(q\) is a number greater than the unit. [D7.2, D7.3, D7.15]

**Step 3.** There is a prime \(r\) measuring \(q\): take \(r=q\) if \(q\) is prime; otherwise \(q\) is composite and VII.31 supplies such a prime. Since \(q\) measures \(d\), and \(d\) measures \(a_n\), repeated multiplication shows that \(r\) also measures \(a_n\). [D7.11, D7.13, 7.31, D7.15]

**Step 4.** Apply IX.12 directly—the natural preceding result here, because it concerns prime divisors of the last term of precisely this kind of progression. It gives that \(r\) measures the term next to the unit, namely \(p\). Since \(p\) is prime and \(r\) is a number, \(r=p\). Thus \(p\) measures \(q\). [9.12, D7.11]

**Step 5.** Write \(q=pt\), where \(t\) is a number or the unit. Then
\[
d=a_k(pt)=(pa_k)t=a_{k+1}t.
\]
Thus \(a_{k+1}\) measures \(d\). This term exists because \(k<n\), and contradicts the choice of \(a_k\) as the last term measuring \(d\). Therefore every number measuring the greatest term has a place among the proportional numbers, as required. [D7.15, D7.20]
statement: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be prime, the greatest will not be measured by any except those which have a place among the proportional numbers.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let N be the least number measured by the given primes p₁, …, pᵣ. Suppose that another prime q, distinct from every pᵢ, measures N. Distinct primes cannot measure one another, since a prime has no numerical measure other than itself. Consequently N ≠ q, for otherwise p₁ would measure q. [D7.11]

**Step 2.** Since q measures N and is less than N, there is a number M such that N = qM. This product consists of as many copies of M as there are units in q. Since q is a number, there is more than one such copy; hence M < N. [D7.5, D7.15, D7.2, CN5]

**Step 3.** Use the prime-divisor-of-a-product theorem directly, since the factorization N = qM already supplies its hypotheses. Each original prime pᵢ measures qM, so it measures either q or M. But pᵢ cannot measure the distinct prime q. Therefore every pᵢ measures M. [7.30, D7.11]

**Step 4.** By Steps 2–3, M is a number less than N measured by all the original primes, contradicting the stipulated leastness of N. Thus N is not measured by any prime except those originally measuring it.
statement: If a number be the least that is measured by prime numbers, it will not be measured by any other prime number except those originally measuring it.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be three numbers in continued proportion, least among those having the same ratios. The direct route is to use the coprimality of the extremes: VIII.3 applies exactly to this hypothesis, so A and C have no common measure except the unit (8.3; D7.12). Moreover, A:B = B:C gives
AC = B²
by VII.19 (7.19).

**Step 2.** Write p | X when p measures X. A measure also measures every multiple, and a common measure of two unequal numbers measures their difference: these facts follow by expressing the numbers as repeated sums of their measure (D7.5; D7.15). If two numbers are not prime to one another, they have a common measure d greater than the unit (D7.12). By VII.32, either d itself is prime or some prime p measures d; hence the two numbers have a common prime measure (7.32). This proposition is used because it applies directly to any common measure. It therefore suffices in each case below to exclude a common prime measure.

**Step 3.** Suppose a prime p measures both A+B and C. Since p measures C, it measures AC = B². By VII.30, applied to B multiplied by itself, p measures B (7.30). Subtracting B from A+B, we find that p also measures A. Thus p measures both A and C, contrary to Step 1 and the definition of numbers prime to one another (D7.12). Therefore A+B is prime to C.

**Step 4.** Suppose a prime p measures both B+C and A. Then p measures AC = B², so VII.30 again implies that p measures B (7.30). Subtracting B from B+C shows that p measures C. This again contradicts the coprimality of A and C (D7.12). Therefore B+C is prime to A.

**Step 5.** Suppose a prime p measures both A+C and B. Then p measures B² = AC. By VII.30, p measures A or C (7.30). If it measures A, subtraction from A+C shows that it measures C; if it measures C, subtraction shows that it measures A. Either way, A and C have a common prime measure, contradicting Step 1 (D7.12). Therefore A+C is prime to B.

Consequently, any two of the three numbers added together are prime to the remaining number, as required.
statement: If three numbers in continued proportion be the least of those which have the same ratio with them, any two whatever added together will be prime to the remaining number.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be numbers prime to one another; thus their only common measure is the unit. Suppose, for a contradiction, that there is a number C such that A:B = B:C. [D7.12]

**Step 2.** Choose the least-numbers route, since it applies directly to the given coprimality. By 7.21, A and B are the least numbers among those having the same ratio as A:B. [7.21]

**Step 3.** The least numbers having a given ratio measure the corresponding numbers having that ratio. Applying this to A:B = B:C, we obtain that A measures B (and B measures C). [7.20]

**Step 4.** Since A also measures itself, A is a common measure of A and B. But A is a number, a multitude of units, not the unit; this contradicts their being prime to one another. Therefore no number C can satisfy B:C = A:B: the second number is not to any other number as the first is to the second. [D7.2, D7.12]
statement: If two numbers be prime to one another, the second will not be to any other number as the first is to the second.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ be numbers in continued proportion, with A₁ and Aₙ prime to one another. Suppose, contrary to the claim, that a number X satisfies Aₙ:X = A₁:A₂. Then A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ, X are in continued proportion. [D7.20]

**Step 2.** We compare the original progression with its one-place shift, since this brings the given coprime extremes directly into the argument. The two lists A₁, …, Aₙ and A₂, …, Aₙ, X have equal corresponding successive ratios. Therefore, ex aequali,
A₁:Aₙ = A₂:X. [7.14]

**Step 3.** Since A₁ and Aₙ are prime to one another, they are the least numbers having their ratio. Consequently, in the proportion just obtained, A₁ measures A₂ and Aₙ measures X the same number of times. In particular, write A₂ = kA₁, where k is a positive integral multiplicity. [7.21, 7.20]

**Step 4.** For every i < n, continued proportion gives A₁:A₂ = Aᵢ:Aᵢ₊₁. By the definition of proportional numbers, Aᵢ₊₁ = kAᵢ. Repeatedly substituting yields Aₙ = kⁿ⁻¹A₁. Thus A₁ measures Aₙ. [D7.20]

**Step 5.** Hence A₁ measures both extremes. But A₁ is a number, not a unit, whereas numbers prime to one another have only a unit as a common measure. This contradicts the hypothesis. Therefore the last number cannot be to any other number as the first is to the second. [D7.2, D7.12]
statement: If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the extremes of them be prime to one another, the last will not be to any other number as the first to the second.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the given numbers, in their given order, be A and B. We seek a number C such that A:B = B:C. Choose the direct product criterion of VII.19, since it applies immediately to these four terms: the required proportion holds if and only if the product of A and C equals the product of B with itself. [7.19]

**Step 2.** Form S by multiplying B by itself. Investigate whether S consists of a whole number of copies of A: subtract A successively, counting the copies removed, until either S is exhausted or a positive remainder smaller than A remains. This process terminates because S is a finite multitude of units and each subtraction removes units. Multiplication is precisely repeated addition, so this procedure tests whether S is a multiple of A and determines its multiplier. [D7.2, D7.15]

**Step 3.** Suppose S is exhausted and the count of copies is a number C. Then C multiplying A produces S; therefore A multiplying C also produces S. Since S is also the product of B with itself, VII.19 gives A:B = B:C. Thus C is the required third proportional. [D7.15, 7.16, 7.19]

**Step 4.** Otherwise no third proportional number exists. For if such a number C existed, VII.19 would make the product of A and C equal to S. By commutativity and the definition of multiplication, S would consequently consist of exactly C copies of A, contrary to the test. This also excludes the boundary case S = A: the count is then only an unit, whereas a number is a multitude of units. [7.19, 7.16, D7.15, D7.1, D7.2]

**Step 5.** Hence the investigation is complete: multiply B by itself and test whether the resulting number is measured by A a number of times, rather than merely once. If so, that number of times is the third proportional; if not, no third proportional number is possible. [D7.15, 7.19]
statement: Given two numbers, to investigate whether it is possible to find a third proportional to them.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the three given numbers, in their prescribed order, be A, B, C. We seek a number D such that A:B = C:D. Choose the direct product route: VII.19 is naturally applicable because it converts precisely this proportionality into equality of two products. Construct P by multiplying B by C. [D7.15, 7.19]

**Step 2.** Suppose a fourth proportional number D exists. By VII.19, the product of A and D equals P. Thus P consists of as many copies of A as there are units in D. Consequently A measures P; moreover, since D is a number—a multitude of units—P is greater than A. These are necessary conditions. [7.19, D7.15, D7.2, D7.5]

**Step 3.** Test these conditions by successively taking copies of A from P. This process terminates, since P consists of finitely many units. If a nonzero remainder smaller than A remains, A does not measure P, so Step 2 excludes a fourth proportional. If P is less than or equal to A, Step 2 likewise excludes a fourth proportional number. Otherwise, if the copies exhaust P, let D consist of as many units as the number of copies taken. At least two copies have been taken, so D is a number, and the product of A and D is P, by the definition of multiplication. Since P is also the product of B and C, VII.19 gives A:B = C:D. [D7.2, D7.15, 7.19]

**Step 4.** Therefore the investigation is complete: a fourth proportional number exists exactly when A measures BC and BC is greater than A; when it exists, construct it by counting how many times A measures BC. The boundary case BC = A yields only a unit, not a number in Euclid’s sense. [D7.5, D7.2, 7.19]
statement: Given three numbers, to investigate when it is possible to find a fourth proportional to them.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let any assigned finite multitude of distinct prime numbers be \(p_1,\ldots,p_r\). Take a number \(M\) measured by every one of them. Such a number is obtained by starting with \(p_1\) and repeatedly applying VII.34 to the preceding common multiple and the next prime. Each earlier prime continues to measure the new common multiple, since a multiple of a multiple consists of repeated groups of the original measure. We use this common-multiple route; minimality is not needed. [7.34, D7.5]

**Step 2.** Add one unit to \(M\), obtaining \(N=M+1\). Since every assigned prime measures \(M\), each is at most \(M\); consequently \(N\) is greater than every assigned prime. [D7.5, CN5]

**Step 3.** If \(N\) is prime, it is therefore a prime outside the assigned multitude. Otherwise \(N\) is composite, and VII.31 supplies a prime \(q\) which measures \(N\). VII.31 is the natural result to invoke here because this branch already assumes that \(N\) is composite. [D7.11, D7.13, 7.31]

**Step 4.** In the composite case, suppose that \(q\) were one of the assigned primes. It would then measure both \(M\) and \(N\). Subtracting the copies of \(q\) composing \(M\) from those composing \(N\) leaves a positive whole number of copies of \(q\); thus \(q\) would measure \(N-M=1\). This is impossible: \(q\), being a number, is a multitude of units, and no positive whole number of copies of it can equal a single unit. Hence \(q\) is not among the assigned primes. [D7.5, CN3, D7.2]

**Step 5.** Thus, in either case, there is a prime distinct from every prime in the assigned multitude. Adjoining it gives a greater multitude of primes. Since the assigned multitude was arbitrary, **prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers**. [Steps 1–4]
statement: Prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A₁, …, Aₙ be any finite collection of even numbers. We take the direct route through the definition of even. Divide each Aᵢ into two equal parts Bᵢ and Cᵢ, so that Aᵢ = Bᵢ + Cᵢ and Bᵢ = Cᵢ. [D7.6]

**Step 2.** Add all the parts Bᵢ together, and separately add all the parts Cᵢ together. Since each Bᵢ equals its corresponding Cᵢ, repeated addition of equals to equals gives B₁ + ⋯ + Bₙ = C₁ + ⋯ + Cₙ. [CN2]

**Step 3.** The whole A₁ + ⋯ + Aₙ consists precisely of these two equal collections of parts. It is therefore divisible into two equal parts and hence is even. Thus, if as many even numbers as we please are added together, the whole is even. [D7.6]
statement: If as many even numbers as we please be added together, the whole is even.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let an arbitrary multitude of odd numbers be given, and suppose their multitude is even. Choose the direct route of removing one unit from each odd number. Each remainder is even, by the definition of an odd number. [D7.7]

**Step 2.** Add all these even remainders together, and call their sum R. The sum R is even, since any multitude of even numbers has an even sum. [9.21]

**Step 3.** Call the sum of the removed units U. There is exactly one removed unit for each given odd number, so U is the number expressing their multitude. Since that multitude is even by hypothesis, U is even. [D7.2]

**Step 4.** The whole sum of the given odd numbers is R together with U. Both are even, so their sum is even. Therefore, if any even multitude of odd numbers is added together, the whole is even. [9.21]
statement: If as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be even, the whole will be even.

proof:
**Step 1.** If there is only one summand, the whole is that given odd number. Otherwise, set aside one odd summand, calling it A. Since the multitude of summands is odd, the multitude remaining after removing one is even. [D7.7]

**Step 2.** Let E be the sum of the remaining odd numbers. By IX.22, E is even. This is the direct route: setting aside one summand reduces the question to the already established even-multitude case. [9.22]

**Step 3.** Since A is odd, it differs by a unit from an even number B. The sum E + B is even, because it is a sum of even numbers. But the required whole E + A differs by that same unit from E + B; therefore it is odd. Thus the sum of any odd multitude of odd numbers is odd. [D7.7, 9.21]
statement: If as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be odd, the whole will also be odd.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let B be the even number subtracted from the greater even number A. We use the definition of evenness directly: divide A into two equal parts and B into two equal parts. [D7.6]

**Step 2.** From each half of A subtract one half of B. These subtractions are possible because B is less than A, so its halves are less than the corresponding halves of A. Since equals have been subtracted from equals, the two remaining parts are equal. Together they constitute exactly the remainder after B is subtracted from A. [CN3]

**Step 3.** Thus the remainder is divisible into two equal parts and is therefore even. Hence, if an even number is subtracted from an even number, the remainder is even. [D7.6]
statement: If from an even number an even number be subtracted, the remainder will be even.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be an even number, B the odd number subtracted from it, and C the remainder; thus A = B + C. By the definitions of even and odd, it suffices to show that C is not even. [D7.6, D7.7]

**Step 2.** Use the preceding subtraction proposition, 9.24, since it applies directly to the same whole with its remainder subtracted. Suppose C were even. Then subtracting C from the even number A would leave an even number. But what remains is B, which is odd—a contradiction. [9.24, D7.6, D7.7]

**Step 3.** Therefore C is not even: it is not divisible into two equal parts, and hence is odd. Thus, if an odd number is subtracted from an even number, the remainder is odd. [D7.6, D7.7]
statement: If from an even number an odd number be subtracted, the remainder will be odd.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be odd numbers, with A greater than B, and let R be the remainder when B is subtracted from A. Thus A = B + R. By the definition of an odd number, write A = E + 1 and B = F + 1, where E and F are even. We choose this direct reduction because removing the common unit turns the given subtraction into an even-from-even subtraction. [D7.7]

**Step 2.** Substituting gives E + 1 = F + 1 + R. Subtracting the same unit from these equal quantities gives E = F + R. Hence R is also the remainder when F is subtracted from E. [CN3]

**Step 3.** Since E and F are even, the remainder when F is subtracted from E is even. Therefore R is even: if an odd number is subtracted from an odd number, the remainder is even. [9.24]
statement: If from an odd number an odd number be subtracted, the remainder will be even.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the given odd number, B the even number subtracted from it, and R the remainder, so that A = B + R. By the definitions, B is divisible into two equal parts, whereas A is not. [D7.6, D7.7]

**Step 2.** Use IX.21, since adding B back to the remainder recovers A. If R were even, then B and R would both be even, and their sum A would be even by IX.21. Thus A would be divisible into two equal parts, contrary to its being odd. [9.21, D7.6, D7.7]

**Step 3.** Therefore R is not divisible into two equal parts and hence is odd. Consequently, if an even number is subtracted from an odd number, the remainder is odd. [D7.6, D7.7]
statement: If from an odd number an even number be subtracted, the remainder will be odd.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the odd number A, by multiplying the even number B, produce C. By the definition of multiplication, C is the sum of as many copies of B as there are units in A. We use this direct repeated-addition route because the number being repeated is already even. [D7.15]

**Step 2.** Each of these copies of B is even. Since the sum of any multitude of even numbers is even, C is even. Therefore, if an odd number multiplies an even number, the product is even. [9.21]
statement: If an odd number by multiplying an even number make some number, the product will be even.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be odd numbers, and let A by multiplying B produce C. By the definition of multiplication, C is the sum of as many copies of B as there are units in A. We choose this direct repeated-addition route because it immediately expresses the product as a sum of odd numbers. [D7.15]

**Step 2.** Each summand B is odd, and their multitude A is odd. Therefore their sum C is odd, since a sum of odd numbers whose multitude is odd is itself odd. Thus an odd number multiplying an odd number produces an odd number. [9.23]
statement: If an odd number by multiplying an odd number make some number, the product will be odd.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the odd number a measure the even number b. Thus b consists of some whole number q of copies of a. Since an odd number cannot equal an even number, more than one copy occurs, so q is a number. In the language of multiplication, q multiplied by a produces b. [D7.3, D7.15, D7.6, D7.7]

**Step 2.** We use the odd-product criterion, since it applies directly to this multiplier q. If q were odd, then q multiplied by the odd number a would produce an odd number, by 9.29. But its product b is even. Therefore q is not odd and hence is even. [9.29, D7.6, D7.7]

**Step 3.** Since q is even, divide its multitude of units into two equal parts. Accordingly, separate the q copies of a making up b into two groups with equally many copies. The sums of these groups are equal, because they are sums of equally many equal numbers; together they constitute b. Each group therefore sums to the half of b. [D7.6, D7.15, CN2]

**Step 4.** Each group consists of a whole number of copies of a, so a measures its sum (with one copy allowed). Consequently a measures the half of b. Therefore, if an odd number measures an even number, it also measures the half of it. [D7.3, D7.15]
statement: If an odd number measure an even number, it will also measure the half of it.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be an odd number prime to a number B. Since A is odd, it cannot be divided into two equal parts. Therefore 2 does not measure A: otherwise A would be twice some number, and its two copies would give two equal parts. [D7.7, D7.15]

**Step 2.** Since 2 consists of two units, its only measures are the unit and 2 itself. As 2 does not measure A, the unit alone is a common measure of A and 2. Thus A and 2 are prime to one another. [D7.2, D7.12]

**Step 3.** Choose the direct product route of VII.24, because both factors B and 2 are now known to be prime to the same number A. By that proposition, their product is also prime to A. This product is B added to itself, hence the double of B. Since being prime to one another is symmetric, A is prime to the double of B, as required. [7.24, D7.15, D7.12]
statement: If an odd number be prime to any number, it will also be prime to the double of it.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A₀ be the dyad, and let A₁, A₂, … be the numbers obtained by successively doubling it, so that Aᵢ consists of two copies of Aᵢ₋₁. The dyad is even, and every Aᵢ is even because it is divided into two equal parts. Fix any n ≥ 1. As throughout Book VII, a number is a multitude of units; the unit itself is not a numerical factor. [D7.1, D7.2, D7.6]

**Step 2.** Aₙ is measured by Aₙ₋₁ according to the dyad. Both Aₙ₋₁ and the dyad are even. Therefore Aₙ is even-times even. [D7.15, D7.8]

**Step 3.** We use descent through the successive halves, since IX.30 applies directly to a proposed odd measure. Suppose an odd number d measures Aₙ. By IX.30 it also measures Aₙ₋₁. Repeating the same argument, since each intervening number is even, d must measure A₀, the dyad. But an odd number, being a multitude of units and not even, contains at least three units. No positive whole number of copies of it can make the dyad. This is a contradiction. Thus no odd number measures Aₙ. [9.30, D7.2, D7.6, D7.7, D7.15]

**Step 4.** In any multiplication of two numbers producing Aₙ, each factor measures Aₙ: this follows from the definition of multiplication and the equality of the products when the factors are interchanged. Neither factor can therefore be odd, by Step 3; hence both are even. Together with Step 2, this shows that Aₙ is even-times even only. Since Aₙ was any number obtained by continually doubling beginning from the dyad, the proposition follows. [D7.15, 7.16, D7.6, D7.7, D7.8]
statement: Each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let N have an odd half H. Thus N is twice H. By the definition of multiplication and interchange of the factors, the dyad measures N according to H. Since the dyad is even and H is odd, N is even-times odd. [D7.15, 7.16, D7.6, D7.9]

**Step 2.** To establish “only,” we use the direct even-sum route. Suppose, contrariwise, that N is also even-times even. Then an even number E measures N according to an even number K: N is the sum of K copies of E. [D7.8, D7.15]

**Step 3.** Since K is even, divide those copies into two groups containing equally many copies. Their sums are equal, so each sum is the half H of N. Each group consists entirely of even numbers; hence its sum H is even by 9.21. If a group contains just one copy, its sum is E itself and is already even. This route applies without needing to determine the parity of half of K. [D7.6, 9.21]

**Step 4.** But H is odd, and therefore is not divisible into two equal parts, whereas an even number is so divisible. This is a contradiction. Consequently N is not even-times even; together with Step 1, this proves that N is **even-times odd only**. [D7.7, D7.6, D7.8, D7.9]
statement: If a number have its half odd, it is even-times odd only.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the given number, and let B be its half, understood in the hypothesis as a number. Since B is not odd, it is even. Thus the even number 2 measures A according to the even number B, so A is even-times even. [D7.6, D7.7, D7.8]

**Step 2.** For the other conclusion, use successive halving directly: the hypothesis excluding continual doubling will exclude termination at the unit. Halve A, and continue halving whenever the result is even. This process terminates, since a number is a finite multitude of units and each halving strictly decreases that multitude. If it terminated at the unit, reversing the halvings would produce A by continual doubling beginning with the dyad, contrary to the hypothesis. It therefore terminates at a number C which cannot be divided into two equal parts; hence C is odd. [D7.1, D7.2, D7.6, D7.7]

**Step 3.** Suppose there were k halvings, and let E be obtained by doubling the unit k times. Reversing the halvings expresses A as C added to itself E times, so E multiplying C produces A. Since at least one doubling occurred, E is divisible into two equal parts and is even. By commutativity of multiplication, C multiplying E also produces A; thus E measures A according to C. [D7.15, D7.6, 7.16]

**Step 4.** Consequently A is measured by the even number E according to the odd number C, and is therefore even-times odd. Together with Step 1, this proves that A is both even-times even and even-times odd. [D7.9, D7.8]
statement: If a number neither be one of those which are continually doubled from a dyad, nor have its half odd, it is both even-times even and even-times odd.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let a₁, a₂, …, aₙ be the given numbers in continued proportion, and let d = a₂ − a₁ and e = aₙ − a₁ be the stated excesses. Put S = a₁ + ⋯ + aₙ₋₁ and T = a₂ + ⋯ + aₙ. We choose the numerical sum-of-antecedents theorem directly, since the adjacent pairs already have equal ratios. From a₁:a₂ = a₂:a₃ = ⋯ = aₙ₋₁:aₙ, it gives a₁:a₂ = S:T. [7.12]

**Step 2.** Alternating this proportion gives a₁:S = a₂:T. [7.13]

**Step 3.** The sums T and S contain the same intermediate terms a₂, …, aₙ₋₁. Cancelling these common terms gives T − S = aₙ − a₁ = e. (For two given numbers, this identity is immediate.) [CN3]

**Step 4.** In the proportion a₂:T = a₁:S, subtract a₁ from the whole a₂ and S from the whole T. Since the subtracted numbers have the same ratio as the wholes, the remainders have that ratio also. Thus (a₂ − a₁):(T − S) = a₁:S, or d:e = a₁:S. [7.11]

**Step 5.** Alternating once more gives d:a₁ = e:S. Therefore, as the excess of the second number over the first is to the first, so is the excess of the last over the first to the sum of all the numbers before the last, as required. [7.13]
statement: If as many numbers as we please be in continued proportion, and there be subtracted from the second and the last numbers equal to the first, then, as the excess of the second is to the first, so will the excess of the last be to all those before it.

proof:
**Step 1.** Write the given doubling progression as
\[
1,2,2^2,\ldots,2^k=a,
\]
and let
\[
p=1+2+2^2+\cdots+2^k,\qquad N=pa.
\]
By hypothesis, \(p\) is prime. Since the unit alone is not a prime number, \(k\geq1\), so \(a\geq2\). Powers here merely abbreviate repeated doubling, and products denote repeated addition. [D7.1, D7.2, D7.11, D7.15]

**Step 2.** For the sum, use the immediately preceding geometric-progression theorem, 9.35. Apply it to
\[
2,4,\ldots,2a,4a.
\]
The excess of the second term over the first equals the first term. Hence the excess of the last term over the first equals the sum of all preceding terms:
\[
4a-2=2+4+\cdots+2a=2p.
\]
Consequently,
\[
p=2a-1.
\]
[9.35, D7.15, CN3]

**Step 3.** The number \(2\) is prime: no number strictly between the unit and \(2\) can measure it. Thus 9.13 applies directly to the original unit-starting progression. Every divisor of \(a\), including the unit and \(a\) itself, therefore belongs to
\[
1,2,2^2,\ldots,2^k.
\]
This is the natural divisor theorem to use because its hypotheses are exactly those of our doubling progression; no general factorization theorem is needed. [D7.2, D7.11, 9.13]

**Step 4.** Let \(d>1\) be any proper divisor of \(N\), and write \(N=dq\), where \(q>1\). Since the prime \(p\) measures \(dq\), 7.30 says that \(p\) measures \(d\) or \(q\).

If \(d=pe\), then \(peq=pa\), so cancellation gives \(eq=a\). Thus \(e\) measures \(a\), and Step 3 gives \(e=2^j\). Since \(d<N\), we have \(j<k\), so \(d=p2^j\).

If \(q=pf\), cancellation in \(dpf=pa\) gives \(df=a\). Thus \(d\) measures \(a\), and Step 3 gives \(d=2^i\), with \(0\leq i\leq k\).

Accordingly, every proper divisor, with the unit included separately, belongs to one of the two lists
\[
1,2,\ldots,2^k
\quad\text{or}\quad
p,2p,\ldots,2^{k-1}p.
\]
[7.30, 9.13, D7.15]

**Step 5.** Conversely, every listed term is a proper divisor of \(N\): the respective complementary factors are \(p2^{k-i}\) and \(2^{k-j}\). There are no repetitions within either list. Nor can the lists overlap, since \(p=2a-1>a\), while every term of the first list is at most \(a\) and every term of the second is at least \(p\). Hence these lists give exactly all the parts of \(N\), each once. [D7.3, D7.15, CN5]

**Step 6.** The first list sums to \(p\). The second sums to
\[
p(1+2+\cdots+2^{k-1})=p(p-a).
\]
Therefore the sum of all the parts of \(N\) is
\[
p+p(p-a)=p(1+p-a)=p\bigl(1+(2a-1)-a\bigr)=pa=N.
\]
Thus the product equals its own parts and is therefore perfect, as required. [D7.15, CN2, CN3, D7.22]
statement: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be set out continuously in double proportion, until the sum of all becomes prime, and if the sum multiplied into the last make some number, the product will be perfect.
